transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah, thanks for seeing me. So, I came in because... well, it's kind of hard to explain, but I've been having this issue with eating that's really starting to freak me out. I work at an entertainment complex—managing the floor, dealing with crowds, making sure the games and attractions are running smoothly—and my shifts usually go pretty late into the night. By the time I clock out, I'm completely drained but also kind of wired from all the noise and the lights, you know? 

So, I'll usually stop to grab some food on the drive back, which makes sense because I'm starving after being on my feet for ten hours. But the problem is what happens when I get home. I'll sit down with a full takeout meal—like a massive double burger, large fries, maybe some nuggets—and I'll finish all of it. But then I just... I keep going. It's like a switch flips in my head. I'll head straight to the pantry and start tearing into bags of chips, cookies, sweets, honestly just whatever is sitting around in the apartment. 

I don't even really feel like I'm tasting it half the time, I'm just pacing around the kitchen or sitting in front of the TV, opening boxes and wrappers. And then, maybe an hour or two later, I sort of snap out of it and look down at the coffee table, and I see all the empty takeout containers and the crushed chip bags, and I am just... I'm shocked. Like, genuinely, physically shocked by how much I just ate. It's just this massive mountain of food for one person, and I don't understand how I'm putting it all away, but it keeps happening after these late shifts, and I just can't seem to stop myself once I start.
Do you usually feel guilty after these episodes of eating a large amount of food?

Guilty? Um... I don't know if guilt is really the right word for it. I mean, I guess people usually feel bad about eating a bunch of junk food, but for me, it's not like I'm sitting there beating myself up or thinking, "Oh, you're a terrible person for eating all this." It's honestly more just... pure confusion. Like, absolute bewilderment. 

Like I was saying, I'll look down at the coffee table—it's this glass-top table I have right in front of my couch, this big brown leather sectional that is incredibly comfortable, which is probably part of the problem because once I sink into it after walking the arcade and laser tag floors all night, my legs are just done and I don't want to get back up. But I'll be sitting there, and my stomach will feel so incredibly stretched out and heavy, just this really uncomfortable, tight physical sensation, you know? And I'll look at the grease stains on the cardboard takeout boxes, and the empty sleeves of cookies—usually I go for those chocolate chip ones with the soft centers, or sometimes the peanut butter wafers—and I just stare at it all and think, "How did that even physically fit inside my stomach?" 

So it's not really guilt, if that makes sense. I'm not crying over it or feeling ashamed of myself in that moment. I just don't understand the mechanics of it. I'll usually just gather it all up in a big plastic garbage bag right then and there because I absolutely hate waking up to a messy living room. Since my shifts usually start later in the day, around 2 or 3 PM, I have all morning to just sit around my apartment, and I don't want to be staring at a pile of wrappers while I'm drinking my morning coffee. So I'll haul it all out to the dumpster behind my building before I even go to bed. But yeah, to answer your question, I haven't really noticed feeling guilty about it. Just really, really baffled by the sheer volume of it all and how I didn't even realize I was doing it until it was over.
Do you feel like you're in control of your eating during these episodes after you get home from work?

Control? Man, no. Not at all. That's actually the part that really messes with my head the most. Because, you know, at work, I'm totally in control. I have to be. I've got, you know, hundreds of kids and teenagers running around the arcade, the laser tag vests need to be charged, the prize counter has to be restocked, the ticket machines jam up, and I'm the one managing all of that. I'm the guy making the calls and keeping the chaos in check. But then I get home, and it's like... I don't even know. It's like I'm a completely different person. 

Once I start eating on those nights, it’s honestly like I’m watching myself from the outside. Like I'm hovering somewhere up near the ceiling fan—which, by the way, I always keep on medium because my apartment gets incredibly stuffy at night, the ventilation in that building is just terrible—and I'm just looking down at myself on the couch. And in my head, my internal monologue is going a mile a minute. I'm literally telling myself to put the food away. I'm thinking, "Okay, that's enough, you finished the takeout, you're full, just close the cookie sleeve. Roll the bag up and put a clip on it." I even have these heavy-duty plastic chip clips, the magnetic ones that stick to the fridge, they're right there in the drawer next to the sink, it would take two seconds to get up and use one. 

But my hands... it's like my hands don't even belong to my brain anymore. They just keep going. They just keep opening containers, ripping into the plastic wrappers, reaching back into the bags, over and over again until everything is gone. Every last crumb. And I'm just sitting there, completely disconnected from my own body, unable to stop my own hands from moving. It's so bizarre because I know I'm doing it, and I'm telling myself to stop, but the physical action just keeps happening anyway. So, yeah, any sense of control is just completely out the window once that switch flips.
Do you feel anxious or stressed while you're eating during these episodes?

Anxious? Stressed? Uh... no, not really. It's not like that. I mean, I know people talk about "stress eating," like when you have a terrible day at work and you just want to eat a pint of ice cream to feel better. But for me, it's not like I'm sitting there feeling wound up or panicked while it's happening. 

Honestly, it's almost the opposite. Like I said, I'm usually coming off a ten-hour shift. By the time I get home, I am just completely physically exhausted. My feet ache, my back aches, my head is usually throbbing from all the flashing lights and the constant noise of the arcade machines and the music they play on a loop over the PA system—it's this playlist of top 40 hits that just repeats every three hours, and by the end of the week, I feel like I'm losing my mind listening to it. So when I finally get through the door of my apartment, drop my keys in the little ceramic bowl by the door, and kick my shoes off, I'm not feeling stressed. I'm just tired. 

And then, when the eating starts... like I was describing, it's just this weird, disconnected feeling. I'm not sitting there crying or worrying about my bills or stressing about work the next day. I'm just kind of... blank. It's like my brain just shuts off, or at least the part of my brain that feels emotions just goes offline for a bit. I'm just watching my hands move, watching myself eat all this food, and I'm not really feeling anything at all in the moment. It's just a mechanical process. Grab the food, open the wrapper, eat it, grab the next thing. So no, I wouldn't say I feel anxious or stressed during it. It's more like I'm just running on autopilot, completely numb to whatever else is going on in my head.
Do you ever make yourself vomit after one of these eating episodes?

Yeah, um... sometimes I do. It's just... well, because like I was saying before about how incredibly full and stretched out my stomach gets, it's just this heavy, rock-solid feeling. And I'll be sitting there on that leather sectional, and the apartment is totally quiet by that point except for the hum of the refrigerator—it's an older model, so the compressor is actually pretty loud when it kicks on in the middle of the night—and I just start thinking about all that food. All those empty takeout containers and the sleeves of snacks and whatever else I just ate. 

And I just... I can't stand the thought of it just sitting in there. You know? Like, my metabolism definitely isn't what it used to be now that I'm forty. I'm on my feet all day at the arcade, sure, but I just know that if I let all that grease and sugar just sit in my stomach overnight while I'm sleeping, it's going to absorb right into me and turn straight into weight. I can almost picture it happening, just sitting there digesting and turning into fat while I'm just lying in bed. 

So, yeah, sometimes after I get home and eat way too much of that takeout or all those snacks, I'll finally force myself up off the couch and go down the hall to the bathroom. It's a really narrow hallway, and the bathroom is right at the end, and the fluorescent light above the mirror in there is super bright, which is honestly awful at 3 AM when your eyes are already tired. But I'll go in there, and I'll lift the lid, and I'll just... make myself throw up. Just to get it out of me. Because if I can just empty it out and flush it away, then I don't have to worry about it sitting in me and turning into all this extra weight. It's just a way to kind of undo the physical damage of it all, I guess.
How often do these episodes of eating a large amount of food happen?

How often... well, if I really sit down and think about the timeline, it's been pretty consistent lately. I mean, ever since I moved into this new apartment—the one with the terrible ventilation and that loud fridge I was telling you about. Moving is just such a massive hassle, you know? I had cardboard boxes stacked up everywhere for the first month, and my schedule was completely thrown off because I was trying to unpack after those ten-hour shifts at the arcade, which is just impossible when all you want to do is collapse. 

But once all the boxes were finally broken down and hauled out to the recycling bin, and the apartment move actually settled into a normal routine... I'd say since then, most weeks I have at least one of these late-night episodes. It's usually just that one night a week where I just completely lose the thread and end up eating way, way past what I ever meant to. 

And then, you know, I have to fix it. I have to do something to make up for it, right? So, like I said, sometimes I'll go down that narrow hallway to the bathroom and try to make up for it by throwing up. But if I don't do that, I still have to compensate somehow. So sometimes I'll just completely skip breakfast the next day. I'll wake up and just drink black coffee—I have this cheap little drip maker on the counter that takes absolutely forever to brew, but it does the job—and I'll force myself not to eat a single thing until much later in the day, even if my stomach is growling while I'm fixing the ticket machines at work. Or, if I don't skip breakfast, I'll force myself to go on a really long run. Which is awful, honestly, because my knees aren't great now that I'm forty, and running on the concrete sidewalks around my complex is just brutal on my joints, but I just feel this intense, overwhelming need to burn it all off. So yeah, at least once a week, it's the eating, and then either the throwing up, skipping breakfast, or just pounding the pavement for miles to try and undo it all.
How often do you make yourself vomit after one of these eating episodes?

Well, the throwing up specifically... I guess I don't do that every single time. It really depends on how the night goes and how I'm feeling about what I just ate. Because, like I said, sometimes I'll try to fix it by just starving myself the next morning with that black coffee, or I'll go for that awful run on the concrete. 

But the vomiting... if I'm looking at just that, I'd say maybe... I don't know, maybe a couple times a month? It's not every week. Sometimes I can just talk myself into doing the running instead, even though I dread it. But other times, if I've eaten something really heavy, like if I got that greasy lo mein from the place on the corner instead of just snacking on chips, I just can't stomach the idea of waiting until morning to burn it off. The thought of it just sitting there, turning into fat while I'm trying to sleep in that quiet apartment with the loud fridge... it just gets in my head. So on those nights, maybe two or three times a month, I'll end up in that bright bathroom doing it. But it's definitely not every single time I overeat. It's just when the panic about it absorbing into my body gets too loud to ignore, you know?
Do you make yourself vomit after these episodes more often than you initially thought, or has it been consistently a couple of times a month?

Well, it's... it's pretty much been consistently a couple of times a month. I mean, I really try to keep track of it, you know? Because it's not something I want to be doing all the time. But it's just... like I was saying, sometimes after I get home and I eat way too much of that takeout, or if I go through all those sleeves of snacks while I'm sitting on the couch, the panic just sets in. 

And I'll be sitting there, and the apartment is so quiet except for that loud refrigerator compressor kicking on and off, and I just start thinking about all that food just sitting in my stomach. Just sitting there, absorbing into my body, turning into weight while I'm trying to sleep. And my metabolism just isn't what it used to be, you know? I'm forty now, and even though I'm on my feet all day at the arcade, fixing the ticket machines and walking back and forth across the floor, it's just not enough to burn off all those calories if I let them sit there overnight. 

So, yeah, on those nights where I just can't handle the thought of it, I'll go down that narrow hallway to the bathroom—the one with the awful, bright fluorescent light—and I'll make myself throw up. Just to get it out of me, so it won't sit in me and turn into weight. But it really is just a couple of times a month. It hasn't increased or anything. It's just when I feel like I really, really need to undo it, and the thought of waiting until morning to go for a run or skip breakfast is just too overwhelming. So I just... I just take care of it right then and there, so I can finally go to sleep without worrying about it.
Do you ever experience a fear of gaining weight or becoming fat?

Oh, absolutely. I mean, it's honestly something I think about all the time, constantly. It's like this background noise that never really goes away, you know? Even when I'm at work, walking around the arcade floor, checking on the Skee-Ball machines or fixing a jammed coin slot, it's just always there in the back of my mind. 

And the funny thing is, people at the venue actually tell me I look too lean sometimes. Like, one of the prize counter girls made a comment last week about how I need to eat a burger or something, which is just... I mean, they don't know what it takes to look like this. They don't know what I'm doing in that bright bathroom at two in the morning. But even with them saying that, I still get so incredibly panicky if my pants feel even a tiny bit tighter when I put them on in the morning. Or if I step on that digital scale I keep tucked under the sink and it's up even just a single pound. 

It's like my heart just drops right into my stomach. Because if it's up a pound, what if it's up two pounds tomorrow? And then what if the guests at the arcade or my coworkers notice right away? I just have this overwhelming fear that they're going to look at me and think, 'Wow, he really let himself go.' Which is ridiculous, I know, because nobody is paying that close attention to the guy fixing the arcade games, but I just can't shake the feeling. I just feel like everyone is judging me, and if I gain weight, it means I've failed, you know? It means I've lost control. So yeah, the fear of getting fat... it's huge. It's probably the main reason I do all of this in the first place, just to make sure that never, ever happens.
How often do you think about your fear of gaining weight?

Well, like I was just saying a minute ago, it's... it's pretty much constant. I mean, from the exact moment I wake up until I finally manage to fall asleep, it's just there. Every single day. Every hour, honestly. I know I just brought up how people at the venue will actually tell me I look too lean sometimes, but it honestly doesn't matter what they say. It doesn't put a dent in how often I worry about it. 

Because the second my work pants feel even a tiny, microscopic bit tighter around the waist when I'm getting dressed, or if I pull out that scale and it's up just one single pound... my whole day is completely hijacked. I'll be at work, walking down the rows of flashing screens, and I just can't stop thinking about it. I'll be bent over fixing a jammed token slot, and my brain is just absolutely convinced that the guests playing the games and my coworkers are all staring at me, noticing that one pound, and thinking I completely let myself go. It's like I'm trapped in this endless loop where I'm constantly scanning my body, constantly terrified that today is the day everyone realizes I'm gaining weight. So, to answer your question, it's not just a passing thought I have every now and then... it's basically the soundtrack to my entire day. I just can't turn it off, no matter how busy I am.
Do you engage in any other compensatory behaviors besides vomiting, such as excessive exercise or fasting, after these eating episodes?

Well, yeah, actually... I do other things besides the vomiting. I mean, the vomiting is just for when I really, really panic at night, but if I don't do that, or even sometimes if I do, I still feel this intense need to... to fix it, you know? Like, to balance the books. So, if I have one of those bad nights where I just eat all that takeout and those snacks, the next morning is... it's like a mission. 

I'll wake up early, even if I'm completely exhausted from tossing and turning all night, and I'll force myself to go out to this dirt trail near my apartment. Usually, I'd just do a couple of miles, but on those mornings, I make myself run extra. Like, I'll push it to five or six miles, even if my knees are aching and my chest is burning, because I just have this voice in my head telling me I have to burn off everything from the night before. And it's not even about enjoying the run; it's purely about punishment, I guess. Or damage control. 

And then, after that, I'll completely skip breakfast before my shift at the arcade. I'll just drink black coffee—like, three cups of it—just to keep my stomach feeling empty and to give me enough energy to get through fixing the machines and dealing with the guests. Even when my stomach is growling so loud I swear the people playing Skee-Ball can hear it, I just won't let myself eat. I'll tell myself, 'You don't deserve breakfast today because of what you did last night.' It just feels like I absolutely have to undo it, you know? Like if I don't run those extra miles or if I eat even a piece of toast, all that food from the night before is just going to permanently attach itself to me. So yeah, I definitely do that... probably more than I should, honestly.
How often do you go for those extra long runs as a way to compensate for the eating episodes?

Well, it's... it's pretty tied to how often those bad nights happen, which, honestly, has been pretty consistent lately. I mean, since I finally got everything unpacked and the apartment move kind of settled into a routine—you know, no more boxes everywhere, finally got my coffee maker set up on the counter—most weeks I have at least one of those late-night episodes. 

Like, at least once a week, I'll be sitting there in the quiet, and I just start eating, and then I eat way, way past what I meant to. It just spirals. And then, because I did that, I have to try to make up for it. So, at least once a week, I'm doing something to fix it—whether that's throwing up in that bright bathroom, or completely skipping breakfast and just surviving on black coffee the next day, or forcing myself out onto that dirt trail for a really long run until my knees are just absolutely screaming at me. 

So, to answer your question about the runs specifically, it just depends on which punishment I end up choosing that morning, but the whole cycle... the eating too much and then having to compensate for it... that's happening at least once a week, pretty much every week since I got settled into the new place. It's just become this exhausting part of my routine now, right alongside going to the arcade and fixing the coin slots.
How often do you skip meals as a way to compensate for these eating episodes?

Well, it's... it's kind of like the running, honestly. It just really depends on how the morning goes and what I feel like I need to do to, you know, fix things from the night before. I mean, I don't really have a set schedule for it, like 'Oh, today is a fasting day.' It's not like that. It's more... reactive? 

Like, if I wake up and I'm just so exhausted from staying up late eating, and the thought of putting on my running shoes and going out to that dirt trail just makes me want to cry, then I'll skip breakfast instead. I'll just drink the coffee. Or sometimes, if I feel really, really guilty—like if it was a particularly bad binge, where I ate the takeout and then got into the snacks I bought for the week—I'll do both. I'll run *and* I'll skip breakfast. 

So, I don't know the exact number of times I skip meals specifically, because it's all just mixed in with the throwing up and the running. It's just part of that whole... that whole weekly cycle I was telling you about. At least once a week, I'm doing *something* to compensate, but whether it's skipping a meal or running, it just varies. I just know that when I do skip breakfast, I'll be at the arcade, fixing a jammed ticket dispenser, and my stomach is just hollow, but I'll tell myself, 'You have to do this, you can't eat until lunch, or maybe even dinner.' It's just... it's whatever I feel like I have to do to make the guilt go away, you know? But as for a specific number of times just for skipping meals... I honestly couldn't tell you. It's just all tangled up together.
How often do you engage in excessive exercise as a way to compensate for these eating episodes?

Well, like I was trying to explain before, it's... it's really hard to separate the running from the other stuff. I mean, since I got all the boxes unpacked and the apartment move finally settled into a routine—which, by the way, took forever because I had to organize all my tools for work and set up my little coffee station just right—but since then, most weeks I have at least one of those late-night episodes. 

You know, the ones where I'm just sitting there and I eat way, way past what I originally meant to. It just happens. And then, because I did that, I have this overwhelming need to make up for it. So, at least once a week, I'm doing *something* to undo it. Sometimes it's throwing up in the bathroom, sometimes it's completely skipping breakfast and just drinking black coffee all morning at the arcade, and sometimes it's lacing up my sneakers and forcing myself out onto that dirt trail for a really long run until my legs feel like they're going to give out. 

But if you're asking me for a specific number of times I *just* run... I can't really give you one. It's like a menu of bad options, and I just pick whichever one I feel like I have to do that morning to balance the scales. But the whole cycle—the eating too much and then doing something, anything, to compensate—that's happening at least once a week, pretty much every week since I got settled. It's all just one big, exhausting blur, honestly.
Do you vomit or use laxatives after eating episodes more often than twice a month?

Well, yeah, I mean... it definitely happens more than twice a month. Like I've been saying, the whole cycle happens at least once a week, and throwing up is... it's definitely one of the main things I do. 

Usually, it's after a shift at the arcade. I'll get off work, and my brain is just buzzing from all the noise, the flashing lights, the kids screaming, fixing the same jammed token machines over and over. I get back to the apartment, and it's so quiet. Too quiet, you know? And I'll order takeout—maybe a massive amount of Chinese food, or pizza, and then I'll get into the snacks I bought for the week, the chips and the cookies. I'll just sit on my couch, and before I know it, I've eaten so much that my stomach physically hurts. It's this heavy, uncomfortable stretching feeling. 

And then the panic sets in. I'll just be sitting there, looking at the empty containers, and I can just feel all that food sitting inside me, and all I can think is how it's going to turn into weight. It's just going to sit there and turn into fat, and I can't stand the thought of it. So, I'll go into the bathroom—the one with the really bright, unforgiving fluorescent light above the mirror—and I just... I make myself throw up. I have to get it out so it won't just sit in me. 

So, yeah, to answer your question, if the whole eating thing happens at least once a week, and I'm choosing between running, skipping meals, or throwing up... throwing up happens pretty often. Definitely more than twice a month. It's just... it's the fastest way to get rid of that heavy, awful feeling and stop it from turning into weight, even though I feel terrible afterwards, just kneeling there on the bath mat. But I just can't let it stay inside me.
How many times in the past month have you vomited after one of these eating episodes?

Well, let's see... in the past month? It's... it's like I was saying before, it's really hard to give you a precise number just for the vomiting because it's all part of this bigger routine I've fallen into. 

Ever since I finally got all the boxes unpacked and the apartment move settled into a routine—which, I mean, that took a whole month on its own just to get my tools organized and the kitchen set up the way I like it—but since then, most weeks I have at least one of those late-night episodes. You know, where I come home from the arcade, everything is just too quiet, and I end up eating way, way past what I originally meant to. I'll start with the takeout, then move to the snacks, and then... then the panic hits. 

And then I try to make up for it. I *have* to make up for it. So I'll either throw up, or I'll skip breakfast the next day and just run on black coffee while I'm fixing the skee-ball machines, or I'll force myself to go on a really long run on that dirt trail until my legs are shaking. 

So if you're looking at just the past month... that's about four weeks, right? And if the whole cycle is happening at least once a week... I don't know, maybe I've thrown up two or three times in the last month? Sometimes it's the running, sometimes it's the skipping meals, and sometimes it's the throwing up. It really just depends on how desperate I feel in that moment, kneeling there in the bathroom with that awful fluorescent light buzzing overhead. I wish I could give you a neat little number, like 'exactly four times,' but it's just... it's a mix of all those things I do to try and fix it. But definitely at least a couple of times this past month, for sure.
Have you vomited after eating episodes more than four times in the past month?

No, no, definitely not more than four times just for the throwing up part. Like I was trying to explain a minute ago, the whole... the whole routine, the eating too much and then doing *something* to fix it, that only happens about four times a month total. Just once a week or so. 

So if I'm splitting that up between the running, the skipping meals, and the throwing up, the throwing up itself isn't happening more than four times. It's just... well, sometimes after I get home from a really long shift—you know, dealing with the ticket counters and the coin jams and the noise all day—and I end up eating way too much of that takeout or all those snacks I keep in the pantry, I just get this overwhelming dread. I'll go into the bathroom and make myself throw up simply so it won't just sit in my stomach. I just can't stand the idea of it sitting in me and turning into weight. That's the whole reason I do it, to stop that from happening. 

But because I also do the running and the fasting on other weeks, the actual vomiting part hasn't been more than four times this past month. It's probably just the two or three times like I mentioned. I just sort of cycle through my options, I guess you could say, depending on how exhausted I am when I get home and how much I ate. If I eat a really heavy meal, the throwing up just feels like the only way to get rid of that weight immediately. But yeah, definitely not more than four times.
Have you vomited or used laxatives after eating episodes more than four times in the past month, on average?

No, not on average, either. I mean, I know we're going over this again, but I really want to make sure I'm explaining it right, because it's complicated, you know? It's not just a simple yes or no. Like I was saying, the whole cycle—the eating and then the panic and then the fixing it—happens about once a week. So that's four times a month, total, for the whole shebang. 

And I've never touched a laxative in my life. The thought of that just... no. So it's just the throwing up, the running, and the fasting. And because I mix it up, depending on how the week went, how my legs feel after standing on the arcade carpet for eight hours, or how heavy the food was... the throwing up itself just doesn't hit that high of a number. 

It's like... okay, sometimes after I get home and eat too much takeout or those snacks I keep in the pantry, I just get this awful, heavy feeling. And I go to the bathroom and make myself throw up simply so it won't sit in me and turn into weight. That's the only reason I do it. I just can't stand the idea of it sitting there. But I don't do that every single time. Sometimes I just wake up the next day and think, 'Okay, I'm just not going to eat today, I'll just drink coffee,' or I'll go run on the trail until I feel like I'm going to collapse. 

So if you're asking if I average more than four times a month for the vomiting... no. It's really just the two or three times, tops. Because if the whole thing only happens four times a month, and I'm doing other things to make up for it half the time, the math just doesn't add up to more than four. I just... I really want to be clear about that, because I know throwing up sounds really bad, and I don't want you to think I'm doing it every single day or anything. It's just one of the tools I use, I guess, when the panic gets too bad and I just need it out of me right then and there.
Have you vomited after eating episodes more than four times in the past month?

I... wait, didn't we just... I feel like we're going in circles a little bit here, Doc. No, I haven't thrown up more than four times in the past month. Like I was trying to explain, it's just not that frequent because of all the other things I do. 

I mean, I get why you're asking, I really do. It's a big deal, the throwing up. It's... it's awful, honestly. But no, it's not more than four times. Sometimes, yeah, after I get home from the arcade and I'm just so wound up from the lights and the noise and the kids screaming, I'll eat way too much of that takeout or the snacks I have stashed away. And then... then that heavy feeling hits. It's like a rock in my stomach, and the panic just washes over me. And in those moments, yeah, I'll go to the bathroom and make myself throw up simply so it won't sit in me and turn into weight. That's the only reason. I just can't stand the thought of it turning into fat. 

But like I said before, I don't do that every time. Sometimes I run, sometimes I just don't eat the next day. So the throwing up part? Definitely not more than four times in the last month. Just two or three times, max. I promise I'm not trying to hide a higher number from you, it's just really not happening more than that.
Have you vomited after eating episodes more than four times in the past month?

I... okay, I know you have a checklist or something you have to get through, but I feel like we are literally just repeating the exact same question over and over again. I don't know how else to say it, but no. No, I have not thrown up more than four times in the past month. 

I feel like I'm not explaining myself right, or maybe you're just not hearing me, but I'll say it again. The whole cycle—the eating too much and then the panic and then the doing something about it—only happens about four times a month total. And because I split that up between the running until my legs feel like they're going to fall off, or just completely skipping meals the next day, the throwing up part just doesn't happen that often. 

I mean, yes, sometimes after I get home from the arcade, and my head is just pounding from the noise and the flashing lights and dealing with people all day, I'll just crash. And I end up eating way too much of that takeout I picked up on the way home, or I just tear through all those snacks I keep in the pantry. And then... then I just get this overwhelming, awful feeling. It's like this heavy dread in my stomach, and I just panic. So I go to the bathroom and make myself throw up simply so it won't sit in me and turn into weight. That is literally the only reason I do it. I just can't stand the idea of it sitting there, turning into fat. 

But I don't do that every single time I eat too much. I really don't. Sometimes I just wake up the next morning and think, 'Okay, I'm just going to drink coffee today and not eat anything else,' or I'll go hit the trail and run for hours. So if you're asking specifically about the vomiting... no, it hasn't been more than four times in the past month. It's really just two or three times, tops. I'm really trying to be honest with you here, and I feel like I'm just saying the same thing over and over. I promise, the number isn't higher than that.

doctor.intent: identify the patient's chief complaint
doctor.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

target_item.name: Eating_Large_Amount
target_item.manifestation: I came in because after late shifts I’ll stop for food and then keep going at home—like a full takeout meal, chips, sweets, whatever’s in the apartment—and afterward I’m shocked by how much I ate.
target_item.reason: This is the first reply of the consultation, so I must return the chief complaint symptom code (S049).

patient.answer:
Hi, yeah, thanks for seeing me. So, I came in because... well, it's kind of hard to explain, but I've been having this issue with eating that's really starting to freak me out. I work at an entertainment complex—managing the floor, dealing with crowds, making sure the games and attractions are running smoothly—and my shifts usually go pretty late into the night. By the time I clock out, I'm completely drained but also kind of wired from all the noise and the lights, you know? 

So, I'll usually stop to grab some food on the drive back, which makes sense because I'm starving after being on my feet for ten hours. But the problem is what happens when I get home. I'll sit down with a full takeout meal—like a massive double burger, large fries, maybe some nuggets—and I'll finish all of it. But then I just... I keep going. It's like a switch flips in my head. I'll head straight to the pantry and start tearing into bags of chips, cookies, sweets, honestly just whatever is sitting around in the apartment. 

I don't even really feel like I'm tasting it half the time, I'm just pacing around the kitchen or sitting in front of the TV, opening boxes and wrappers. And then, maybe an hour or two later, I sort of snap out of it and look down at the coffee table, and I see all the empty takeout containers and the crushed chip bags, and I am just... I'm shocked. Like, genuinely, physically shocked by how much I just ate. It's just this massive mountain of food for one person, and I don't understand how I'm putting it all away, but it keeps happening after these late shifts, and I just can't seem to stop myself once I start.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient experiences guilt after binge eating
doctor.question: Do you usually feel guilty after these episodes of eating a large amount of food?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of guilt after binge eating episodes, which is not explicitly covered by any of the specific symptom profiles provided (e.g., S049 Eating_Large_Amount, S050 Loss_of_Control, S048 Compensatory_Behavior_Purging). While guilt is a common feature of Bulimia Nervosa, it does not have a dedicated key in the provided list.

patient.answer:
Guilty? Um... I don't know if guilt is really the right word for it. I mean, I guess people usually feel bad about eating a bunch of junk food, but for me, it's not like I'm sitting there beating myself up or thinking, "Oh, you're a terrible person for eating all this." It's honestly more just... pure confusion. Like, absolute bewilderment. 

Like I was saying, I'll look down at the coffee table—it's this glass-top table I have right in front of my couch, this big brown leather sectional that is incredibly comfortable, which is probably part of the problem because once I sink into it after walking the arcade and laser tag floors all night, my legs are just done and I don't want to get back up. But I'll be sitting there, and my stomach will feel so incredibly stretched out and heavy, just this really uncomfortable, tight physical sensation, you know? And I'll look at the grease stains on the cardboard takeout boxes, and the empty sleeves of cookies—usually I go for those chocolate chip ones with the soft centers, or sometimes the peanut butter wafers—and I just stare at it all and think, "How did that even physically fit inside my stomach?" 

So it's not really guilt, if that makes sense. I'm not crying over it or feeling ashamed of myself in that moment. I just don't understand the mechanics of it. I'll usually just gather it all up in a big plastic garbage bag right then and there because I absolutely hate waking up to a messy living room. Since my shifts usually start later in the day, around 2 or 3 PM, I have all morning to just sit around my apartment, and I don't want to be staring at a pile of wrappers while I'm drinking my morning coffee. So I'll haul it all out to the dumpster behind my building before I even go to bed. But yeah, to answer your question, I haven't really noticed feeling guilty about it. Just really, really baffled by the sheer volume of it all and how I didn't even realize I was doing it until it was over.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient experiences a loss of control during the eating episodes
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're in control of your eating during these episodes after you get home from work?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: Once I start on those nights, it’s like I’m watching myself from the outside, telling myself to put the food away, but my hands just keep opening containers until everything is gone.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking if I feel like I'm in control of my eating during these episodes, which corresponds to the Loss of Control symptom.

patient.answer:
Control? Man, no. Not at all. That's actually the part that really messes with my head the most. Because, you know, at work, I'm totally in control. I have to be. I've got, you know, hundreds of kids and teenagers running around the arcade, the laser tag vests need to be charged, the prize counter has to be restocked, the ticket machines jam up, and I'm the one managing all of that. I'm the guy making the calls and keeping the chaos in check. But then I get home, and it's like... I don't even know. It's like I'm a completely different person. 

Once I start eating on those nights, it’s honestly like I’m watching myself from the outside. Like I'm hovering somewhere up near the ceiling fan—which, by the way, I always keep on medium because my apartment gets incredibly stuffy at night, the ventilation in that building is just terrible—and I'm just looking down at myself on the couch. And in my head, my internal monologue is going a mile a minute. I'm literally telling myself to put the food away. I'm thinking, "Okay, that's enough, you finished the takeout, you're full, just close the cookie sleeve. Roll the bag up and put a clip on it." I even have these heavy-duty plastic chip clips, the magnetic ones that stick to the fridge, they're right there in the drawer next to the sink, it would take two seconds to get up and use one. 

But my hands... it's like my hands don't even belong to my brain anymore. They just keep going. They just keep opening containers, ripping into the plastic wrappers, reaching back into the bags, over and over again until everything is gone. Every last crumb. And I'm just sitting there, completely disconnected from my own body, unable to stop my own hands from moving. It's so bizarre because I know I'm doing it, and I'm telling myself to stop, but the physical action just keeps happening anyway. So, yeah, any sense of control is just completely out the window once that switch flips.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's eating episodes are accompanied by a sense of anxiety or stress
doctor.question: Do you feel anxious or stressed while you're eating during these episodes?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of anxiety or stress during the eating episodes, which is not specifically covered by any of the symptom profile items. The closest items (Eating Large Amount and Loss of Control) have already been addressed, and Fear of Weight Gain relates to body image and weight, not the emotional state during the binge.

patient.answer:
Anxious? Stressed? Uh... no, not really. It's not like that. I mean, I know people talk about "stress eating," like when you have a terrible day at work and you just want to eat a pint of ice cream to feel better. But for me, it's not like I'm sitting there feeling wound up or panicked while it's happening. 

Honestly, it's almost the opposite. Like I said, I'm usually coming off a ten-hour shift. By the time I get home, I am just completely physically exhausted. My feet ache, my back aches, my head is usually throbbing from all the flashing lights and the constant noise of the arcade machines and the music they play on a loop over the PA system—it's this playlist of top 40 hits that just repeats every three hours, and by the end of the week, I feel like I'm losing my mind listening to it. So when I finally get through the door of my apartment, drop my keys in the little ceramic bowl by the door, and kick my shoes off, I'm not feeling stressed. I'm just tired. 

And then, when the eating starts... like I was describing, it's just this weird, disconnected feeling. I'm not sitting there crying or worrying about my bills or stressing about work the next day. I'm just kind of... blank. It's like my brain just shuts off, or at least the part of my brain that feels emotions just goes offline for a bit. I'm just watching my hands move, watching myself eat all this food, and I'm not really feeling anything at all in the moment. It's just a mechanical process. Grab the food, open the wrapper, eat it, grab the next thing. So no, I wouldn't say I feel anxious or stressed during it. It's more like I'm just running on autopilot, completely numb to whatever else is going on in my head.

doctor.intent: determine presence of compensatory behaviors
doctor.question: Do you ever make yourself vomit after one of these eating episodes?

target_item.name: Compensatory_Behavior_Purging
target_item.manifestation: Sometimes after I get home and eat too much takeout or snacks, I go to the bathroom and make myself throw up so it won’t sit in me and turn into weight.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking if the patient makes themselves vomit after binge eating, which corresponds to purging compensatory behaviors.

patient.answer:
Yeah, um... sometimes I do. It's just... well, because like I was saying before about how incredibly full and stretched out my stomach gets, it's just this heavy, rock-solid feeling. And I'll be sitting there on that leather sectional, and the apartment is totally quiet by that point except for the hum of the refrigerator—it's an older model, so the compressor is actually pretty loud when it kicks on in the middle of the night—and I just start thinking about all that food. All those empty takeout containers and the sleeves of snacks and whatever else I just ate. 

And I just... I can't stand the thought of it just sitting in there. You know? Like, my metabolism definitely isn't what it used to be now that I'm forty. I'm on my feet all day at the arcade, sure, but I just know that if I let all that grease and sugar just sit in my stomach overnight while I'm sleeping, it's going to absorb right into me and turn straight into weight. I can almost picture it happening, just sitting there digesting and turning into fat while I'm just lying in bed. 

So, yeah, sometimes after I get home and eat way too much of that takeout or all those snacks, I'll finally force myself up off the couch and go down the hall to the bathroom. It's a really narrow hallway, and the bathroom is right at the end, and the fluorescent light above the mirror in there is super bright, which is honestly awful at 3 AM when your eyes are already tired. But I'll go in there, and I'll lift the lid, and I'll just... make myself throw up. Just to get it out of me. Because if I can just empty it out and flush it away, then I don't have to worry about it sitting in me and turning into all this extra weight. It's just a way to kind of undo the physical damage of it all, I guess.

patient.answer:
How often... well, if I really sit down and think about the timeline, it's been pretty consistent lately. I mean, ever since I moved into this new apartment—the one with the terrible ventilation and that loud fridge I was telling you about. Moving is just such a massive hassle, you know? I had cardboard boxes stacked up everywhere for the first month, and my schedule was completely thrown off because I was trying to unpack after those ten-hour shifts at the arcade, which is just impossible when all you want to do is collapse. 

But once all the boxes were finally broken down and hauled out to the recycling bin, and the apartment move actually settled into a normal routine... I'd say since then, most weeks I have at least one of these late-night episodes. It's usually just that one night a week where I just completely lose the thread and end up eating way, way past what I ever meant to.

I'll wake up and just drink black coffee—I have this cheap little drip maker on the counter that takes absolutely forever to brew, but it does the job—and I'll force myself not to eat a single thing until much later in the day, even if my stomach is growling while I'm fixing the ticket machines at work. Or, if I don't skip breakfast, I'll force myself to go on a really long run. Which is awful, honestly, because my knees aren't great now that I'm forty, and running on the concrete sidewalks around my complex is just brutal on my joints, but I just feel this intense, overwhelming need to burn it all off. So yeah, at least once a week, it's the eating, and then either the throwing up, skipping breakfast, or just pounding the pavement for miles to try and undo it all.

But the vomiting... if I'm looking at just that, I'd say maybe... I don't know, maybe a couple times a month? It's not every week. The thought of it just sitting there, turning into fat while I'm trying to sleep in that quiet apartment with the loud fridge... it just gets in my head. patient.answer:
Well, yeah, I mean... it definitely happens more than twice a month. Like I've been saying, the whole cycle happens at least once a week, and throwing up is... it's definitely one of the main things I do. 

Usually, it's after a shift at the arcade. I'll get off work, and my brain is just buzzing from all the noise, the flashing lights, the kids screaming, fixing the same jammed token machines over and over. I get back to the apartment, and it's so quiet. Too quiet, you know? And I'll order takeout—maybe a massive amount of Chinese food, or pizza, and then I'll get into the snacks I bought for the week, the chips and the cookies. I'll just sit on my couch, and before I know it, I've eaten so much that my stomach physically hurts. It's this heavy, uncomfortable stretching feeling. 

And then the panic sets in. I'll just be sitting there, looking at the empty containers, and I can just feel all that food sitting inside me, and all I can think is how it's going to turn into weight. It's just going to sit there and turn into fat, and I can't stand the thought of it. So, I'll go into the bathroom—the one with the really bright, unforgiving fluorescent light above the mirror—and I just... I make myself throw up. I have to get it out so it won't just sit in me. 

So, yeah, to answer your question, if the whole eating thing happens at least once a week, and I'm choosing between running, skipping meals, or throwing up... throwing up happens pretty often. Definitely more than twice a month. It's just... it's the fastest way to get rid of that heavy, awful feeling and stop it from turning into weight, even though I feel terrible afterwards, just kneeling there on the bath mat. But I just can't let it stay inside me.
